title: France halts use of stun grenades after boy's hand blown off in student protests
content: France has suspended the use of stun grenades for policing student protests that have swept the country, after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off earlier this week. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said he had requested the pause until the facts of Monday's incident in Lens had been "clarified", with conflicting accounts offered by protesters and officials. The disruption continued on Wednesday with more than 500 schools fully or partially shut. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has defended the police response, after several groups complained of police using disproportionate force towards teenagers. In an address to the nation on Wednesday evening, he denied security forces had "orders to confront" the young people. He said the government would look into the demands made by students and promised they would present a set of proposals at the end of October, ranging from renovating buildings to make more teachers available. He gave no further details. The "anger of young people does not come from nowhere," he said. Education Minister Édouard Geffray said 24 schools had been "set alight or vandalised" to such an extent that they would be shut for several weeks, affecting 30,000 pupils. Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets on Tuesday to call for better school conditions and in some cities tear gas and water cannon were deployed. The interior ministry said 488 people were arrested and 43 members of the security forces were hurt. Nuñez told French radio RTL that police watchdog IGPN had opened 18 investigations to determine whether officers had been "proportionate" during the demonstrations, which have spread from high school pupils to their parents, university students and unions. "There is a police action that raises questions for all of us within the Ministry of the Interior; it's what happened in Lens," he said as he confirmed the suspension of stun grenades - weapons which are considered non-lethal and send out small rubber pellets when they detonate. The 15-year-old boy's hand was torn off after a so-called anti-encirclement grenade was fired in unclear circumstances near the Auguste Béhal high school in the northern city near Lille. Authorities have said he picked up the grenade which then exploded, but students have alleged he was hit directly after an officer fired. According to the local prefect, police had been confronted by more than 200 students throwing stones and fireworks. The national secretary of policing union UNSA said he was sceptical about the move, saying it had been based "on emotion". "We are dealing with increasingly violent people," Jean-Paul Nascimento told FranceInfo, cautioning that without the weapon to disperse crowds there may be more clashes at close quarters. "That's where there will perhaps be even more injuries," he warned. Concerns have also been stoked by the case of a 14-year-old hit in the face with a tear gas grenade last week. The boy's lawyer said he had lost several teeth and suffered a fractured jaw in the incident at Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, north-west of Paris, and a police officer has been charged. And in a separate development on Wednesday, a 16-year-old suffered a serious hand injury outside a school in Strasbourg, reportedly while handling a mortar firework. Prosecutors also said an investigation for attempted murder had been opened after a 17-year-old student protester complained an officer "held his head underwater" while trying to arrest him near a river in the north-eastern city of Belfort. French reports say the boy has himself been charged with aggravated assault for allegedly attacking the officer. Addressing France's National Assembly on Wednesday, both Nuñez and Education Minister Geffray said the speed at which the protests had turned violent was unprecedented. Geffray said dozens of headteachers and deputies had been injured, many deliberately so, and alleged the movement had been "very quickly infiltrated by ultra-violent groups". "We have never seen anything like this," he said of the disorder which officials report has harmed more than 200 students and 700 police officers, and prompted more than 6,600 arrests. Nuñez later said he found it "excessive to speak of police repression of the movement", insisting that officers were only acting in response to violence and damage. The national coordinator of the radical-left France Unbowed (LFI) party said that it had taken "several children being maimed for life for Nuñez to give up using grenades against high school students". The prime minister has accused LFI of trying to "sow chaos" during the protests ahead of elections to select President Emmanuel Macron's successor in April. Its leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon is currently second in the opinion polls behind Marine Le Pen of the hard-right National Rally - who on Wednesday said Macron was "always on the side of attacking the police". The president held an emergency meeting late on Tuesday with Prime Minister Lecornu and other key ministers to find a way out of the crisis after almost a quarter of all lycées were disrupted by the day's protests - with government figures putting the number of protesters at more than 250,000. Lecornu announced that schools should set aside half the day for students to voice their concerns, and noted on social media that an online consultation seeking their opinions had drawn 30,000 responses within a day. But students' unions - who put the number of protesters at 450,000 - maintain a fourth round of demonstrations is planned for Thursday in Paris and other cities, and told reporters they had requested a meeting with Lecornu due to a lack of "concrete measures" outlined so far. The union representing school leaders told FranceInfo that a solution would require "something more than simple consultation periods", while the head of the USL high school union, Ryad Rani, told French radio on Wednesday: "We are telling M. Nuñez, calm your police officers down and call for restraint." The adventurer is walking home to Hull after setting off on his global adventure in 1998. France has halted the use of stun grenades after a 15-year-old boys hand was blown off during student protests. Hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets across France amid a wave of protests by high-school pupils. The adventurer is nearing the end of his 28-year journey home to Hull from Chile. Crowds of mainly teenagers called for more resources for schools and an end to what they called police repression. title: Canada suspends plans to expand assisted dying to people with mental illness
content: Canada says it will indefinitely suspend plans to expand its medically assisted dying law to people whose sole condition is mental illness, citing a lack of consensus on who would be eligible. It comes after a parliamentary panel earlier this year recommended that medically assisted dying - known as Maid in Canada - should not be expanded. On Wednesday, Canada's justice minister, Sean Fraser, said that "while there is not a perfect consensus on this issue, we believe this is the correct approach at this particular time". Supporters of extending the programme to those with mental illness alone argue that not doing so violates their constitutional rights and access to healthcare. A federal case remains before the courts challenging the government's earlier decision to delay access to Maid for people with mental illness. Fraser acknowledged this is an issue that the Supreme Court could weigh on in the future. Wednesday's announcement means that Canadians with mental illness as their sole condition will not be able to access assisted dying by March 2027 as previously planned. The government will instead introduce a new law in the coming weeks that suspends that expansion indefinitely, Fraser said. That proposed legislation will also to allow patients who have a progressing incurable illness to consent to assisted dying before their health deteriorates to the point where they are unable to do so. However, it will leave the final decision up to individual provinces. Advanced requests are not currently legal under federal law, but are allowed in Quebec for those with serious and incurable illnesses. "These are not easy decisions but we believe they will be the correct ones," Fraser said. Medically assisted dying became legal in Canada in 2016 for people with terminal illnesses, who still account for the vast majority of cases. Following a court case in Quebec, it was expanded in 2021 to people with incurable conditions but whose death was not imminent. In Canada, that mechanism is known as "track two" Maid. Canada was first set to expand its assisted dying laws to people whose sole condition is mental illness in 2023, but it delayed doing so twice to allow for time to study its potential delivery. Advocates for expanding assisted dying to people with mental illness alone say they should have the same rights as patients with other types of illness. But concerns have been raised about whether mental illnesses are currently understood well enough by medicine to determine appropriate eligibility. "When I hear that there is a lack of consensus in the medical community about the irremediable nature of certain mental illnesses, that gives me real cause for concern," Fraser said. Claire Brosseau, a woman with treatment resistant bipolar 1 disorder who is part of the federal case challenging Canada's current laws, told the BBC earlier this year that assisted dying would offer her "a safe death". Brosseau's lawyer, Michael Fenrick, told the BBC on Wednesday that the government's decision is "deeply disappointing". "People will continue to suffer intolerably while the case goes through the courts," he said. More broadly, some experts have also raised concerns that Canada's assisted dying programme has become a tool to alleviate the suffering of people who would be better served by improved access to affordable housing and healthcare, and not an option of last resort. In a report earlier this year, a parliamentary committee noted competing opinions on the issue but recommended Canada "indefinitely exclude persons whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness" from assisted dying. It added that there is a "pressing need for increased and more equitable access to adequate mental health services". The conclusions were made after committee members heard from doctors, advocates and experts from countries that do allow assisted dying for people solely with mental illness, like the Netherlands and Belgium. Not all committee members agreed with its recommendation, and some released a dissenting report arguing the process was "fundamentally flawed" and "biased". Polls suggest the majority of Canadians support access to medically assisted death but that support falls it comes to patients with mental illness alone. More than 2,000 people signed an open letter calling for a doctor-led Urgent Treatment Centre in Rugby. A Russian lab technician has died at a plague research centre in Siberia, but there are many reasons pneumonic plague is usually easily contained. The Anchor Centre was meant to open in 2020 but spiralling costs and problems have put that back to 2027. Care should focus on healthy eating and exercise, not medicines such as weight-loss injections, says the World Health Organization Jamie Richards and Joe Dean raise more cash while checking the machines they have already funded. title: Children killed while they slept as Russian missile kills 19 in block of flats
content: A Russian missile has killed 19 people including five children in an apartment block in northern Ukraine, destroying 30 flats as families slept. Three of the children were one-year-olds in the attack on Pryluky, east of Kyiv, early on Wednesday, and one of the boys died with his mother and grandmother, officials said. Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky said it was one of Russia's "most vile strikes", and suggested the Russian military had carried it out as a "birthday gift" to Vladimir Putin, who turned 74 on Wednesday. Moscow made no mention of the attack on Pryluky but said its "massive strike" had targeted military industries in Kyiv and elsewhere. Across the country, the death toll on Wednesday climbed to 25, as Russian strikes claimed two lives in the capital, two in Kremenchuk, and two more in Oleksandriya. More than 430 apartments and private homes were damaged and dozens of people were injured in the attack on the central city of Kremenchuk, the regional leader said. Rescue teams in Pryluky spent hours searching for victims in the rubble of a five-storey block of flats. Late in the afternoon rescuers said the body of a fifth child had been found at the scene. More than 50 residents were wounded in the attack that also damaged other residential buildings as well as a youth centre. Chernihiv regional head Vyacheslav Chaus said the town was hit by five cruise missiles, one of which slammed into the apartment building. Zelensky named the one-year-old victims as Oleksandr, Kyrylo, and Serhii, and said a boy of eight called Maxsym had also been killed. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said a boy called Sasha had died with his mother, Kateryna and her mother Viktoriia, and only the boy's elder sister Olha had survived. Local reports said they had lived on the fifth floor and that Viktoriia had been looking after her grandson while her daughter worked in a factory. "The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively," Zelensky said, adding that 70 missiles were fired in total. Zelensky added that Ukraine had itself struck targets in attacks on Russia's Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions in the past 24 hours, adding there was "also a response in the Black Sea", without providing further details. In Kyiv, many residents spent the night in underground stations to escape the Russian barrage. Mayor Vitaly Klitschko said last week the capital was being torn apart by Russian attacks . Ukraine's national police posted pictures online showing what it says is an unexploded Russian Iskander missile in the middle of a Kyiv district. BBC Verify has confirmed the images are genuine and the apparent missile fragments came down in an area of open land surrounded by high-rise apartment buildings. Another verified video shows damage to cars and what appears to be rubble and a fallen tree in an area surrounded by apartment blocks in Kremenchuk. Ukraine's air force said it had succeeded in shooting down five ballistic missiles and 39 cruise missiles and more than 100 drones, including 46 of Russia's jet-powered drones which have caused so much damage in recent weeks. However, that would mean that as many as 26 cruise or ballistic missiles penetrated its defences, and Zelensky renewed a call for allies to provide air defence support packages to Ukraine. According to Zelensky, one of the "key targets" of the attack was Ukraine's energy infrastructure, which Moscow earlier said it would intensify strikes on following Ukraine's strikes on Moscow's energy facilities. In a separate post on Wednesday, Zelensky said Ukraine had struck four targets in retaliatory attacks in the past 24 hours, including two oil facilities and a training ground as well as a target in the Black Sea. On Tuesday evening, footage emerged showing a huge plume of smoke engulfing an oil tanker off the coast of Sochi, along the Black Sea in southern Russia. The Russian transport ministry later said unmanned boats had attacked the Liberian-flagged Aframax Rio oil tanker. Authorities claim the crew was rescued. Separately, Bulgaria has halted a search for the missing crew of a ship that sank after being hit by a drone on Tuesday, Vice-Admiral Rumen Nikolov from the Maritime Administration Executive Agency said, as reported by Bulgaria's BTA news agency. No details of the crew are known, but Nikolov said it was assumed there were Syrians on board. Tracking data shows the ship was anchored at the southern end of the Bosphorus strait until Monday when it entered the Black Sea heading north. Its last reported position on ship-tracking site MarineTraffic was at 23:43 GMT on Monday in what is known as the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone of the Black Sea. Bulgarian specialist news outlet Maritime.bg reported the Alfa Watan was attacked by a drone and sank 70nm (130km) east of Byala. As well as the civilian cargo ship, a second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, its Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Tuesday. The 18 crew members on the second vessel were rescued. Bulgaria has not said who it believes was behind the attacks, and Moscow has not commented on the incident. Russia has intensified strikes in the Black Sea, particularly the eastern side, as part of its war against Ukraine. In an evening address on Tuesday, Zelensky claimed Russia was responsible for the attacks. Additional reporting by BBC Verify It is not clear who is behind the attacks which come as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea as part of its war against Ukraine. Ukrainians travelling by train are increasingly caught in the crosshairs of Russia's attacks. Arkadii Petrov - who attended Kirkcudbright Academy - is honoured at the Ukrainian Chapel in Lockerbie. BBC Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson is near Kyiv's Northern Bridge, which has been hit for the second day in a row. title: The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope
content: As US President Donald Trump hits the campaign trail in the final sprint to the midterm elections, he is launching an emphatic defence of America's economic performance, trying - as he often does - to bend reality to his will. "We have the best economic numbers of any president in the history of our country, and yet people don't know about it because the press won't talk about it," he said last week. While some economic indicators, including roaring stock market indexes and low US poverty rates, are indeed historic, the overall picture is not nearly as rosy. Trump is often dismissive of concerns about aﬀordability and the high cost of living in the US, describing them as "fake" and a Democrat-inspired "hoax". The American public, however, sees it differently - and some key economic indicators provide ample evidence for their discontent. Inflation remains high at 3.4%, outpacing wage growth. The average cost of petrol has soared to $4.37 (£3.30) a US gallon and beef prices are at a record high. According to a YouGov survey, 63% of respondents believe the economy is "getting worse". An AP/NORC poll released last week found just 17% of adult Americans approve of the president's handling of cost-of-living issues, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall. Those polls also suggest that many of Trump's policies, including tariffs, aggressive immigration enforcement and the ongoing conflict with Iran, are widely unpopular. "We ask our voters their motivation to turn out, and what we find is cost of living, cost of living, cost of living," said Avery James, the director of communications at the Republican-aligned polling company Echelon Insights. "That's the top issue." That has left Republicans running for office in the Congressional elections on 3 November with an agonising choice - should they be distancing themselves from Trump? Their fear is that by echoing his sunny outlook they risk losing a number of electoral races that are currently projected to be very tight. But they also know that being seen to break with the president on the state of the economy is far from consequence free. There are few Republican politicians as loyal to the president as Floridian House Congressman Byron Donalds. And there are few US states as traditionally hospitable to Republicans as Florida. But even in the president's adopted home, which he carried in each of his three elections and which hasn't had a Democratic governor since 1999, candidates like Donalds are finding themselves having to adapt their pro-Republican messaging to acknowledge economic concerns. Donalds - who stood by Trump as he fought his way back to power after his 2020 election defeat and took a prominent role in his 2024 election campaign - is now running for governor of Florida, with Trump's encouragement and enthusiastic endorsement. When I saw him at a Hispanic church in Kissimmee, he was preaching to the proverbial choir - but pitching his message with a nod to the fact that for many money is currently tight. "We're the best state in America," he said before acknowledging: "But success has gotten expensive." He ticked through a laundry list of Florida constituents – retirees, teachers, emergency workers, restaurant staff and local government employees, flagging that they need to be able to "make ends meet". In his stump speech, Donalds didn't mention Trump at all. He leaned heavily into stories of his own financial hardship during his younger years, of living paycheque to paycheque and waiting tables at the traditional southern style restaurant chain Cracker Barrel. When he invited audience questions, there were the usual cultural hot-button topics, like the perceived threat of Sharia law in America, transgender athletes in women's sports and youth crime in public spaces. But his supporters also wanted to talk about the high cost of housing - insurance, taxes, mortgage rates and home-owner fees - and healthcare worker shortages. Trump may have mocked the term affordability, but Donalds – who is criss-crossing the state on an "affordability tour" – isn't the only Republican candidate talking about high prices. It was a similar track at a campaign event in a Tampa seafood market the next day, when Bryan Avila, who is running for lieutenant governor on the same ticket as Donalds, took questions on energy prices and data centre construction. "Everything is going up in prices, from food to even books for people going to college," said John Carroll, who serves on a Florida county housing commission. "It's a challenge no matter which party is in power, but here in Florida it's been Republican for so long." Meanwhile in Texas, Governor Greg Abbott last month went to Texarkana to host a "rural affordability roundtable". "We must lower costs for Texans in every corner of our state, and with my affordability agenda we will help make Texas the most affordable state in America." And in Iowa, Ashley Hinson, a Republican congresswoman running for Senate, unveiled her own "affordability agenda". "Iowans are paying the price for Washington's failures, and they deserve real relief that actually lowers costs," she said. Hinson also recently called for the president to quickly end the Iran war – a sentiment echoed by Republican Senate candidates in Ohio and Michigan. Two of Hinson's Iowa colleagues in the House of Representatives went so far as to vote for a Democratic-backed measure to curtail Trump's war powers in Iran. For the past two years it has been Republicans who control the levers of power in the nation's capital – from the White House to both chambers of Congress. Inevitably, that makes for a challenging rhetorical pirouette among Republican candidates this time round when it comes to touching on Trump's less popular policies. Even Donalds has faced allegations that he is trying to open daylight between himself and Trump. The media was awash in reports recently that he had removed most prominent mentions of Trump from his campaign website. It was a story Donalds quickly denied – and one that prompted an angry response from the president himself. "Another Fake Story is that a very close friend of mine, a man I endorsed very early, Byron Donalds, is taking me off his website and campaign materials," Trump posted on his Truth Social website. "If Florida thought the story that Byron 'dropped' me was true, he would lose the election, and that would be a terrible thing because he's going to be a fantastic governor!" Donalds did say, however, that when it comes to addressing how to tackle high prices, Trump shouldn't be a factor. "That's not even about President Trump," he told reporters after the website story broke. "I'm the one asking for the votes for the people of Florida to be their governor." While Donalds and Trump remain tight, the same cannot be said for Republican candidates who have gone farther in their criticism. Congresswoman Maria Salazar aired a television spot in which she bluntly said Trump's immigration crackdown had "gone too far". Trump reposted a handful of messages on Truth Social accusing the Cuban-American Salazar of betrayal and calling for her to drop out, while other potential candidates had been on the receiving end of his anger during the primaries. According to Marc Short, a Republican strategist and former chief of staff to Donald Trump's first vice-president, Mike Pence, it's hard not to see Trump's move as a warning directed at any other Republicans who might consider a public break with him. But he adds that Trump's ire isn't the only reason Republican candidates should approach this strategy with caution. "It's almost disingenuous now to try to create separation," he says. "I think for voters it looks opportunistic." Candidates like Salazar, who have stuck with Trump for years, have little choice but to rise and fall with the president's fortunes, he said. Republicans who have built their own brand and identities – like Senator Susan Collins in Maine – can more convincingly draw distinctions between themselves and the president. The fact that so many people are downbeat about the economy, combined with the fact that the Republicans have been in power in Washington suggests that Republican candidates are facing difficult headwinds in November's elections. "I think they're hurricane force right now," said Short. It is, however, far from a lost cause for Republicans going into these midterms. Many polls show battleground congressional and state races in a dead heat. And while Democratic candidates' hopes are buoyed by so many people feeling the economy is not working for them, a majority of voters still have a negative view of the Democratic Party as a whole. "I think Republicans are closing out on the fact that they've delivered on a bunch of things, but we need to do more," said Alex DeGrasse, a Republican campaign consultant with close ties to the party's congressional leadership. His recommendation for the Republican electoral message was simple and pointed: "If you elect the Democrats, they'll destroy everything. Democrats had a chance to run the country, and by every objective economic metric, they did a worse job." He added that right now in the White House, Republicans aren't panicking, they're focusing on executing their strategy. In Florida's governor race, the Republican messaging contrasts the "Florida dream" of economic growth that Republicans say they delivered versus what they say is the hardship and depravity of Democratic-run states like Illinois, California and New York. Florida's population is booming, and many of the new arrivals are conservatives who lived in - and grew tired of - more liberal states in the north and west. But even this pitch often came with a nod to the current economic difficulties. "For the past 26 years, we have been living in a Florida dream, and a lot of people don't realise the amount of work that has been done in this state," Avila said in Kissimmee last week. According to James, from the Republican-aligned polling firm, the key for conservative candidates is to take subjects on which they are relatively strong, like crime, taxes and immigration, and link them to affordability issues that Americans say they care about most. "Republicans are certainly looking to tell those independents that you might not be happy with everything, but we have delivered on these issues," he said. With Republicans pouring money into advertising in battleground states, often outpacing their Democratic opponents by significant margins, there's still the possibility that the situation will improve in the final month of the midterm campaign. That hasn't stopped the Republican faithful from being nervous about their side's chances, though – and what some see as a lack of enthusiasm on the right. "Campaigns are won at the end by momentum," said Joseph Robinson, an engineer who attended the Avila fish-market event in Tampa. "But the momentum has been slow. It's not really like, 'Hey, I'm going to go run out there and vote right now.'" Trump, for his part, is inevitably upbeat. Last month, he travelled to Tennessee for a college football game, where the crowd of more than 100,000 greeted him with cheers. The next day, it was a golf tournament in Illinois and another welcoming crowd. This weekend, he's going to another football game - in Alabama. He is hitting the campaign trail, but frequently in states that mostly return Republican candidates – Texas, Oklahoma and Nebraska. However, in classic Trump style, he is saying and doing things that could complicate the careful balancing act many Republicans are trying to strike. He has repeatedly dismissed claims that high costs are a problem for many voters, with his latest explanation being that their discomfort is due to a "very bad job" on the part of his administration in explaining how good things really are. "The only thing we're doing badly at is public relations," he said in Texas last week. "In other words, we're doing a phenomenal job." Several times over the past few months he's insisted that voters imagine his name is "on the ballot", but at other times he has said he doesn't care about the midterms and that this isn't his election to fight. If Republicans struggle, he said, it is not a reflection on how Americans view him. "A lot of them are very angry at Republicans, to be honest with you," Trump said in August. "They're angry at Republicans, but they're not angry at me." But if Republicans get punished at the ballot box in November, whether they run with the president or away from him, Trump will bear the brunt of the consequences - in the form of a hostile Congress with legislative and oversight powers - for the last two years of his presidency. title: Watch: Why family who lived at site of 7 October attack want to return
content: As Israel marks the third anniversary of the 7 October Hamas attacks, the BBC has visited residents of kibbutz Nir Oz - one of the worst hit places. Sitting just a mile (1.6km) from the Gaza border, 41 Nir Oz residents and foreign workers were killed along with six people who had fled to the kibbutz from a party nearby. Seventy-six people from the kibbutz were kidnapped to Gaza, including nine bodies. Fourteen of those hostages were taken alive and killed in captivity. During the 7 October attack, about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage. The ensuing war between Israel and Hamas has killed more than 74,200 people in Gaza according to the Hamas-run health ministry – whose overall figures are seen as accurate by the UN. Read more about this story here. The BBC reports from a school in Taiz, Yemen, where children are determined to keep learning despite the vicious civil war. In rare access to Yemen's conflict zone the BBC travels to the front line with pro-government soldiers. BBC Verify explains how we found the wreckage location of a Saudi F-15 fighter jet which the Iran-backed Houthi group says it shot down over Yemen. Yemen's Houthis have seized territory near the Bab al-Mandab Strait - a key trade gateway for oil and global shipping. Omar al-Bayoumi has always denied being an extremist and a Saudi spy. Washington announced what it described as an "economic D-Day" against Iran, widening current sanctions and targetting countries with business ties with the regime. Mojtaba Khamenei hasn’t been seen in public since March - but AI-generated images of him continue to spread online. The BBC's chief international correspondent looks at how Iran's new leadership will respond to several issues affecting the country. The US has launched the strikes on Iran in response to attacks on three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. Huge crowds have lined the streets of Tehran for the funeral procession of Iran's late supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The BBC's chief international correspondent Lyse Doucet is in Tehran, where funeral events are taking place in honour of Iran's former leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Authorities expect up to 20 million people to attend ceremonies across Iran and Iraq over the coming days. Iranian authorities say they expect millions of people to take part in funeral commemorations for Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Dozens of boats are still anchored in the Strait, while ordinary Iranians try to continue to their lives. The BBC’s Daniel Bush is traveling with Secretary of State Marco Rubio as he seeks to reassure Gulf allies over the Iran deal aimed at ending the war. BBC correspondent Jessica Parker explains some key points of the direct talks between the US vice-president and Iran. The BBC’s Shaimaa Khalil was outside the Iran v New Zealand opening round match as protesters called for an end to Tehran’s clerical regime. It's not clear if the deal means the Israelis will pause their offensive in Lebanon, BBC international editor Jeremy Bowen reports. In a call with the US president, the BBC’s Sarah Smith asked Trump about the war in Iran and his relationship with the Israeli leader. The BBC's international editor, Jeremy Bowen, said the public are "right to be worried" as the consequences of the war will be felt for generations. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: California pair charged with abusing at least 14 surrogate-born children
content: A California pair has been charged with multiple counts of abusing at least 14 surrogate-born children - some as young as two months old - and dissuading a witness. "The number of children who were subjected to this alleged horrific abuse is unprecedented," Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan J Hochman said in a statement. Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang, who US media describe as a couple, were arrested at their Arcadia mansion on Tuesday. The pair pleaded not guilty at a Pasadena courthouse, the BBC's US partner CBS News reported. Xuan, 66, and Zhang, 39, are accused of conspiring to subject 15 of the 16 children living in their home to repeated physical abuse, after 21 children were removed from their custody last year. The pair ran their own surrogacy company and are accused of making false statements to at least two women who became surrogates, indicating that Zhang was struggling to conceive, according to the criminal complaint. As of May 2025, Zhang maintained a spreadsheet that tracked 21 children, including those born to surrogates. Officials said the investigation began that month when Zhang brought a two-month-old boy to the hospital with a head injury, telling medical staff that the baby had fallen from a bed. The couple's lawyer Mitchell Krems said the allegation was a "mischaracterisation" based on the evidence he has reviewed, CBS News in Los Angeles reported. Hospital staff informed law enforcement, and when police arrived at their home they discovered three different rooms called "learning centres" under the supervision of multiple nannies, which Hochman described as a "house of horrors". The mansion allegedly had 32 motion-activated cameras which Hochman said were used by the couple to monitor the discipline given by the nannies. Footage allegedly shows the nannies spanking, slapping or hitting the children. One nanny, Chunmei Li, is accused of hitting the two-month-old baby who suffered the head injury two days before he was brought to the hospital. Krems said Li was quickly fired, CBS News LA reported. Li, 58, was previously charged with one felony count of child abuse under conditions likely to cause great bodily injury or death. Hochman said she was on the run with a $105,000 (£88,800) warrant for her arrest. In July 2025, the couple's home was first raided by authorities, who took 21 children into state custody. Arcadia Police Department said at the time the couple's house was first raided that the children ranged in age from two months to 13 years old, but most were between one and three years old. Fifteen of the children were taken from the couple's home while six others were living elsewhere and also later taken into custody. Krems said his client Xuan was innocent. "He is being targeted for exercising his constitutional right to have a large family," CBS News quoted the lawyer as saying. Investigators believe the surrogate mothers were from around the country and they were unaware they were carrying embryos for the couple at the same time. Melissa Brisman, the attorney for two of the surrogates, told CBS News: "This is wonderful news that people will be held responsible for their actions and there will be consequences if you abuse the surrogacy system". If convicted as charged, Xuan faces a possible maximum sentence of 17 years and four months in state prison, while Zhang faces up to 11 years and eight months. Li faces up to 12 years. title: What the Paramount and Warner Bros deal means for you
content: Paramount Skydance has officially taken over Warner Bros Discovery in a $110bn merger that is set to reshape Hollywood and the media landscape. The merger comes after months of legal disputes and widespread criticism over feared cuts and how consolidation could harm competition and consumers. The newly merged entertainment giant will be rebranded as Skydance, and it will bring together a host of entities including HBO, CBS, Nickelodeon, Showtime, Comedy Central, DC Studios and Food Network. The BBC's Samira Hussain explains what happens now after this historic merger between two of the biggest studios in Los Angeles. title: Watch: Riot police clash with school protesters and use tear gas in France
content: Hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets across France, as a wave of protests by high-school pupils spread to their parents, university students and unions. Crowds of teenagers marched from the Place de la République in Paris, calling for more resources for schools, and what they called less repression from police. Police clashed with demonstrators in Lyon, used tear gas in Paris and Marseille and water cannon in Rennes, but there was little of the serious trouble that marred previous protests. The BBC's Europe correspondent Nick Beake reports from Lille. The US and Russia have each offered to help each other tackling infectious diseases. A series of measures to tackle the housing crisis were defeated in parliament on Friday Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez says the situation in Catalonia remains "very complicated". BBC Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson is near Kyiv's Northern Bridge, which has been hit for the second day in a row. The BBC's Guy Hedgecoe is in Madrid, where a series of marches have been scheduled, after Spain's Congress rejected measures aimed at tackling the country's housing crisis.
